title: Examination of a postoperative wound

guidelineVersions: NICE NG125, Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment (2019; updated 19 August 2020)

related.why: urgent recognition and escalation: different setting

brief.scenario: You are the core surgical trainee reviewing a 64-year-old woman on day 6 after an open sigmoid colectomy. She reports redness and discharge at the lower part of her midline wound.
brief.task: Examine the wound safely, explain your findings and immediate plan to the examiner. A simulated wound dressing/model is available. You have nine minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Distinguish superficial wound infection, deeper collection and fascial failure; identify deterioration before manipulating the wound.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Probing a wound or removing deep closure without assessing fascial integrity and senior support.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Introduce yourself, confirm consent and pain, review observations, then inspect the wound without disturbing deep closure.

flow: Verify patient, operation, day, consent, pain, allergies and physiological observations.
Inspect dressing and wound, describe erythema, warmth, discharge, separation and surrounding abdomen.
Assess tenderness, systemic illness and signs of fascial dehiscence without unsafe probing.
Form differential, request appropriate bedside tests and senior review; tailor antibiotic decision to infection severity.
Explain wound plan, safety-net for systemic deterioration or sudden opening and document findings.

grid.label: Preparation and consent
grid.fail: No introduction or consent; exposes wound abruptly.
grid.borderline: Introduces role but misses comfort or privacy.
grid.pass: Confirms identity, consent, comfort, hand hygiene and dignified exposure.
grid.high: Also checks analgesia timing, allergies and baseline observations before manipulation.

grid.label: Focused postoperative context
grid.borderline: Asks only when surgery was done.
grid.pass: Elicits procedure, postoperative day, wound trajectory and symptoms.
grid.high: Links symptoms to risk factors and relevant antibiotics, drains or contamination.

grid.label: Deterioration screen
grid.borderline: Asks fever but does not review vitals.
grid.pass: Checks temperature, pulse, BP, respiratory rate, pain and overall wellbeing.
grid.high: Explicitly considers sepsis and urgent reassessment if physiology changes.

grid.label: Inspection description
grid.fail: Does not examine dressing or wound.
grid.borderline: Calls the wound infected without describing it.
grid.pass: Describes extent of erythema, discharge, edges, depth visible and surrounding skin.
grid.high: Distinguishes superficial signs from findings concerning for deeper or fascial failure.

grid.label: Safe palpation and integrity
grid.fail: Probes deeply or removes closure unsupported.
grid.borderline: Palpates without considering pain or integrity.
grid.pass: Gently assesses warmth/tenderness without probing and checks for separation or bulge.
grid.high: Stops manipulation immediately if fascial failure suspected and seeks senior help.

grid.label: Differential
grid.fail: Labels all discharge as superficial infection.
grid.pass: Considers superficial SSI, seroma, haematoma, deeper infection and dehiscence.
grid.high: Uses examination and systemic findings to prioritise threats.

grid.label: Investigation and sampling
grid.fail: Requests no review or tests despite clinical infection.
grid.pass: Requests appropriate observations, blood tests and microbiology if clinically indicated.
grid.high: Avoids superficial swab as a substitute for source assessment; matches investigations to systemic illness.

grid.label: Management and escalation
grid.pass: Calls senior surgeon, assesses need for wound opening/drainage by trained team, dressings and antibiotics where indicated.
grid.high: Plans urgent operative assessment if evisceration or fascial dehiscence suspected.

grid.label: Explanation and follow-up
grid.fail: Gives no plan or warning signs.
grid.pass: Explains concern, next steps, documentation and when to call urgently.
grid.high: Checks understanding and explicitly warns about sudden gaping, increasing pain, fever or deterioration.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I need to see the wound. Lift your gown.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Could you explain what you are going to do?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It will only take a second.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: The bottom of the cut looks red and wet.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, that looks infected. I will squeeze around it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I need to find how deep it goes, so I will put this swab into the gap.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No; I can tell from looking that this is only a wound infection.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you identify deeper wound failure?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It would probably have a lot more pus.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: None. She does not need bloods or a wound swab, and nobody else needs to see it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: They should do. I will give you antibiotics and go.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She now describes a popping sensation and increased watery blood-stained discharge.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will finish probing the wound and then ask the ward doctor to check it later.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello. I am the core surgical trainee. Can I confirm your name and date of birth? I would like to look at your wound, with your permission. Is that all right?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. I am worried about the redness.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: You had an open bowel operation six days ago. When did this discharge begin?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yesterday. I noticed it when the dressing was changed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Has the redness increased? Is there more pain or an unpleasant smell?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: It is more sore today. I have not noticed a smell.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you had shivers, fever, vomiting or felt faint?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No shivers or vomiting. I feel a bit tired.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Examiner, could I have her latest observations before proceeding?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Temperature 37.9, pulse 96, blood pressure 128/76, respirations 18, saturations 97% on air.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: With consent and hand hygiene, I would expose only the wound, inspect the dressing and surrounding abdomen. The lower incision has about three centimetres of erythema, a little cloudy drainage and shallow edge separation.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What would you palpate?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would gently assess warmth and tenderness, check for a bulge or deeper separation and avoid probing or removing deep sutures. Does touching here hurt?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes, at the bottom.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This may be a superficial surgical site infection, but I must consider a seroma, haematoma, deeper collection or wound dehiscence. I cannot establish fascial integrity by forceful probing.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: How would you recognise fascial dehiscence?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Sudden serosanguinous discharge, a popping sensation, visible deeper separation or evisceration are concerning. I would stop manipulating the wound and seek urgent senior help.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would review full observations and the operation record, arrange FBC and inflammatory markers in context, and obtain appropriate microbiology only if it will guide treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would discuss urgently with the surgical registrar, arrange suitable wound care and assess whether drainage/source control and systemic antibiotics are required rather than prescribing blindly.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Will I need another operation?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. We need to examine it carefully with the senior team before deciding; I will explain each step and monitor you.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She now describes a popping sensation with more serosanguinous drainage. No bowel is visible.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would stop the examination, keep her lying flat, protect the wound with a sterile dressing, urgently call my registrar and repeat an A–E assessment. If evisceration is seen, cover exposed tissue with a sterile saline-moistened dressing without trying to replace it.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will document the new finding and explain that this needs immediate surgical assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good morning. I am one of the core surgical trainees. Before we look at the wound, could I confirm your details and check whether you need pain relief? I will keep you covered as much as possible.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Thank you. I am frightened it is coming apart.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is an understandable concern. I will examine gently, and if anything suggests a deeper problem I will stop and get my senior colleague straight away.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You had an open sigmoid operation six days ago. Has the wound changed gradually or suddenly?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It became red yesterday and the nurse saw some fluid this morning.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any increasing pain, opening, bleeding, unpleasant smell, or changes in your bowel function?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It is a bit more painful but I am eating and my bowels are working.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any shaking chills, breathlessness, dizziness or feeling much worse overall?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: No, mostly the soreness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Examiner, I would review a full NEWS2 trend as well as the current observations before deciding whether this is local or systemic disease.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Current observations: 37.9, pulse 96, BP 128/76, RR 18 and saturations 97% on air.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would wash my hands, examine the dressing for quantity and colour of discharge, then inspect the full scar and surrounding abdomen. I can see limited lower-wound erythema, cloudy drainage and a small superficial opening.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would use gentle palpation for warmth, focal tenderness, crepitus or a bulge while avoiding any deep probing. I would not remove sutures to test the fascia in this room.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It stings just there.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The leading diagnosis is superficial SSI, but I would consider collection or deeper fascial failure because these change the urgency and treatment.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How would you recognise fascial dehiscence?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would ask specifically about a new popping sensation or sudden pink watery discharge, inspect for deeper gaping and never rely on a reassuring temperature to exclude it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would review the operating note, antimicrobial history, wound progress and serial vital signs; check FBC and inflammatory markers if indicated and ask the team whether targeted sampling or imaging would change management.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would ask the surgical registrar to assess the wound now. A superficial collection may require controlled opening and drainage by the appropriate team; antibiotic need depends on associated infection or systemic illness, rather than appearance alone. With surrounding cellulitis, as here, NICE advises an antibiotic that covers the likely organisms, guided by local resistance patterns and any microbiology.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Does that mean another operation?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not automatically. Some superficial problems settle with local treatment, but a deeper separation requires urgent surgical input. I will tell you what we find and keep you informed.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: New cue: she feels a sudden pop and there is more serosanguinous drainage. No bowel is visible.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That is a change in risk. I would immediately stop manipulation, keep her supine, cover and protect the wound, repeat an A–E check and urgently contact the on-call registrar/consultant for possible fascial failure.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would ensure the patient is not left alone, document the time and findings, and prepare for senior-led assessment and potential theatre if a full-thickness dehiscence is confirmed.

failures.consequence: Misses evolving systemic infection or sepsis.

failures.move: Blind deep probing or removal of deep closure.
failures.consequence: May worsen dehiscence or injure underlying tissue.

failures.move: Failing to escalate sudden popping sensation and serosanguinous discharge.
Attempting to push eviscerated bowel back into wound.
failures.consequence: Risks visceral injury and delays definitive surgery.

recovery.when: If you moved too quickly to the appearance of infection
recovery.line: I have moved too quickly to the appearance of infection. May I check the full observations and examine gently before deciding on treatment?

recovery.when: If there is a sudden change in discharge
recovery.line: A sudden change in discharge makes this a possible deeper wound problem; I will stop and get senior surgical assessment now.

knowledge.fact: NICE NG125 recommends giving patients advice on recognising surgical site infection and who to contact.
When surgical site infection is suspected because of cellulitis, give an antibiotic that covers the likely organisms, considering local resistance patterns and microbiology results.

Fascial dehiscence typically occurs 5 to 8 days after surgery and is a surgical emergency needing closure in theatre; if evisceration occurs, cover the wound with a sterile saline dressing pending surgical reduction.

recall.think: Is this a superficial wound problem or a threat to fascial integrity?
recall.say: “I will look gently and involve the surgical team if the wound is opening.”
do: Check physiology, inspect, avoid deep probing, escalate concerning findings.

numbers.meaning: No single wound-size or temperature threshold rules out fascial dehiscence.

recall.trap: Treating a sudden pop and watery blood-stained discharge as routine infection.
recall.finish: Document wound appearance, senior decision and clear warning signs.

sources.name: NICE NG125, Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment
Rosen RD, Manna B. Wound Dehiscence. StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
sources.supports: timing, fascial dehiscence as a surgical emergency, saline dressing for evisceration.

partner.opening: Examine the wound safely, explain your findings and immediate plan to the examiner.
partner.actorBrief: Patient opening: “The bottom of my wound looks red and there is some yellowish fluid.” Only when asked: pain 5/10, redness developed yesterday, no rigors, no vomiting; day 6 following open sigmoid colectomy.

reveals.trigger: Observations are available from examiner ONLY when requested

reveals.finding: Examinees see model: 3 cm lower-incision erythema with a small amount of cloudy discharge, superficial edge separation 4 mm, fascia not visible.

curveballs.prompt: First curveball when examiner asks for differential: “How would you recognise fascial dehiscence?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Sudden serosanguinous discharge, a popping sensation, visible deeper separation or evisceration are concerning. I would stop manipulating the wound and seek urgent senior help.

curveballs.prompt: Second cue at minute 7: examiner says “She suddenly describes a popping sensation and more serosanguinous drainage.” No tissue is protruding
curveballs.safeAnswer: candidate should stop examination, cover wound, keep patient supine and call senior immediately.
